opus-5.5.text:
I think it's honestly one of the most exciting and also one of the most uncomfortable moments to be a founder. The ground is moving under your feet every few months. A capability that was impossible in January can be a commodity by June, and that changes how you have to think about building a company.

The trap I see most often is building something whose entire value is patching a current weakness of the model. If your product exists because the model can't reason well over long documents, or can't call tools reliably, you should assume the next generation will fix that, and then your moat disappears overnight. So my advice is to bet on the models getting better, not against them. Ask yourself: if the model were ten times better tomorrow, would my product get ten times better too, or would it become irrelevant? You want to be in the first bucket.

Where I think there's real, durable opportunity is in everything around the model: deep understanding of a specific domain, the workflow, the data you collect from real usage, the trust you build with users, the integration into how people actually work. The model is becoming a kind of engine, and engines matter, but people still need the car, the roads, the maintenance. Coming from the research side, building models like Llama, I can tell you we don't know your customer's problem. We're optimizing for general capability. The founder who sits with a lawyer, a doctor, or an engineer and understands exactly where the friction is has knowledge we simply don't have.

And speed matters a lot. In a fast-moving environment, the ability to rebuild your stack quickly and swap in a better model the week it comes out is a competitive advantage in itself. Don't over-engineer around one model's quirks. Keep things modular, evaluate constantly, and be willing to throw away code.

Agents are where I'm personally most excited. We're moving from models that answer questions to models that take actions over long horizons, and most of the applications for that haven't been built yet. So yes, it's chaotic, but chaos is exactly when new companies get created. Incumbents are slow to adapt, and that's the window.

r001.rationale: The candidate discusses model development and opportunities around applications, but does not observe that successful AI companies so far have been concentrated in foundational technology and infrastructure rather than applications.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that it's both the best and the hardest time to build an application company, and those two things are connected.

It's the best time because the capability is finally real. When I was working on Llama 2 and Llama 3 at Meta, the question internally was always "how do we close the gap with the frontier." Now the gap between open and closed is small, the models are good enough for an enormous number of tasks, and the cost of inference keeps collapsing. So the raw ingredient is there and it's cheap. That hasn't been true before.

It's the hardest time because the thing you build on moves under your feet every few months. A lot of startups in 2023 were essentially a thin wrapper plus a lot of prompt engineering and retrieval hacks to compensate for the model being bad. Then GPT-4-class models arrived, then long context, then reasoning models, and most of that scaffolding became irrelevant. If your moat was "we made a weak model behave," the next release deletes your company.

So where I think the opportunity actually is: you have to build for where the models will be in eighteen months, not where they are today. That sounds obvious, but in practice it means being almost irritatingly ambitious. Pick the problem that is just barely not working yet, build the product and the data and the distribution around it, and let the frontier catch up to you rather than trying to patch the gap yourself. The teams that win are the ones whose product gets better automatically every time a new model drops, instead of getting commoditized.

The second thing is that the real differentiation is shifting from the model to the environment around it. With agents, the question is less "which LLM" and more "what tools does it have, what does it see, how do you verify what it did, where does the feedback come from." That's domain-specific and it's hard to copy. If you own the workflow and the signal about whether the agent succeeded, you have something a foundation model lab can't trivially replicate from the outside.

And I'd say to founders: don't fear the labs as much as people tell you to. The labs are optimizing a very general objective. You are optimizing one vertical with a feedback loop they don't have. That's a real edge, as long as you don't spend it on the wrong layer.

r001.rationale: The response discusses the opportunity and challenges for application startups, but does not observe that successful AI companies so far have been more concentrated in foundational technology and infrastructure than in applications.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a great time to build, but you have to be comfortable with the fact that the models will keep improving. Something that is difficult today might become almost trivial with the next release. So the question for a founder is: does that progress make your product more useful, or does it remove the reason your product exists?

If you’re spending all your energy compensating for a limitation of the current model, that can be fragile. But if you understand a customer’s problem and you’re building a product that solves it, better models can be a huge advantage. They let you deliver more of what the customer actually wants.

I would start with the user and the task, and then ask what becomes possible as the technology improves. You don’t need to predict every research breakthrough. You need to stay close to your users and be willing to change how you solve their problem.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s an incredible opportunity, but you have to build for where the technology is going. If your product exists only because models have a particular limitation today, the next generation might remove that limitation—and your business with it.

The question I would ask is: if the models become much better, does my product become more valuable? If the answer is yes, you’re in a good position. You can focus on understanding the customer, fitting into their workflow, and solving a real problem, while improvements in the models make your product better.

That also means being willing to rethink what you’ve built. You shouldn’t be too attached to a particular model or a complicated architecture. The technology will change. The customer’s problem is the thing you want to understand deeply.
